Finding and reading clusters

Source: vignettes/articles/finding-and-reading-clusters.qmd

This guide covers the second step of the pipeline: detecting clusters in a network and interpreting them. It starts from the bibliographic coupling network of the explanations of the 1970s stagflation built in the first guide.

library(networkflow)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidygraph)

nodes <- subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation")
network <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1
)

What is a cluster?

In a bibliographic coupling network, a group of documents that cite the same literature, much more among themselves than with the rest of the network, is the usual operational definition of a research specialty or a research front (Morris and Van der Veer Martens 2008; Boyack and Klavans 2010). Detecting such groups without deciding them in advance is the task of community detection (Fortunato 2010). The algorithms differ, but most formalise “more ties inside than outside” with the modularity of a partition (Newman and Girvan 2004):

Q=12m∑i,j(Aij−γkikj2m)δ(ci,cj), Q = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i,j} \left( A_{ij} - \gamma \frac{k_i k_j}{2m} \right) \delta(c_i, c_j),

with AijA_{ij} the weight of the edge between documents ii and jj, kik_i the total weight of the edges of ii, mm the total weight of the network, δ(ci,cj)=1\delta(c_i, c_j) = 1 when ii and jj are in the same cluster, and γ\gamma the resolution. The term kikj/2mk_i k_j / 2m is the weight expected between ii and jj if edges were placed at random given each node’s weight: a partition has a high modularity when clusters gather much more weight than expected by chance.

Detecting clusters with Leiden

add_clusters() gives access to five algorithms of igraph. The Leiden algorithm (Traag et al. 2019) is the default choice of recent bibliometric work. It improves on Louvain (Blondel et al. 2008) by guaranteeing that clusters are connected, and iterating it keeps refining the partition.

network <- add_clusters(
  network,
  clustering_method = "leiden",
  objective_function = "modularity",
  resolution = 1,
  seed = 123
)

Each document gets a cluster_leiden identifier and the share of the network that its cluster represents (size_cluster_leiden). Edges get the cluster of their two ends, or “00” when they connect two clusters.

node_table <- as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")
sort(table(node_table$cluster_leiden), decreasing = TRUE)

01 02 03 04
69 51 18  9

Resolution and the number of clusters

The partition depends on γ\gamma: a higher resolution makes the expected weight larger and favours more, smaller clusters. Modularity also has a resolution limit: in large networks, it can merge small communities that are clearly separated (Fortunato 2010). A network can legitimately be described at several levels of detail, from fields to specialties (Sjögårde and Ahlgren 2020), and choosing the resolution is choosing the level of the study. A scan of resolutions shows how the number of clusters reacts.

Leiden is also stochastic: two runs with different seeds can give different partitions. A partition we can trust should come back from one seed to the next. The adjusted Rand index (ARI) measures the agreement between two partitions, from about 0 (no more than chance) to 1 (identical). We run Leiden with ten seeds for each resolution and compare each partition with the one of the first seed.

scan <- expand.grid(resolution = seq(0.5, 2, by = 0.25), seed = 1:10)
memberships <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(scan)), function(i) {
  clustered <- add_clusters(
    network,
    clustering_method = "leiden",
    objective_function = "modularity",
    resolution = scan$resolution[i],
    seed = scan$seed[i],
    verbose = FALSE
  )
  as.integer(as_tibble(clustered, active = "nodes")$cluster_leiden)
})
scan$n_clusters <- sapply(memberships, function(m) length(unique(m)))
scan$ari <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(scan)), function(i) {
  reference <- which(scan$resolution == scan$resolution[i] & scan$seed == 1)
  igraph::compare(memberships[[i]], memberships[[reference]], method = "adjusted.rand")
})
scan_summary <- aggregate(cbind(n_clusters, ari) ~ resolution, data = scan[scan$seed != 1, ], FUN = mean)
scan_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(resolution = scan_summary$resolution, value = scan_summary$n_clusters, measure = "Mean number of clusters"),
  data.frame(resolution = scan_summary$resolution, value = scan_summary$ari, measure = "Mean ARI with seed 1")
)
ggplot(scan_long, aes(resolution, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = scico::scico(1, palette = "batlow", begin = 0.3), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = scico::scico(1, palette = "batlow", begin = 0.3), size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Resolution", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

The number of clusters grows steadily with the resolution, and most resolutions give partitions that the seed hardly changes. Where the ARI drops, the algorithm hesitates between partitions of similar quality: results at that resolution should be read with care. A reasonable practice is to choose a resolution in a stable range, to report it, and to check that the clusters a narrative relies on survive at close values (Traag et al. 2013).

Modularity or CPM?

Leiden can also maximise the constant Potts model (Traag et al. 2011), which compares the internal weight ece_c of each cluster with γ\gamma times its number of pairs: H=∑c[ec−γ(nc2)]H = \sum_c [e_c - \gamma \binom{n_c}{2}]. A cluster is worth creating when its density exceeds γ\gamma. Unlike modularity, CPM does not depend on the size of the network, which helps when comparing clusters across networks of very different sizes, as time windows often are. But γ\gamma then lives on the scale of the edge weights:

summary(igraph::E(network)$weight)
    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.
0.005403 0.023470 0.038993 0.052589 0.066302 0.399613 
cpm <- add_clusters(network, clustering_method = "leiden", objective_function = "CPM",
                    resolution = 1, seed = 123, verbose = FALSE)
length(unique(as_tibble(cpm, active = "nodes")$cluster_leiden))
[1] 147

With weights around 10−410^{-4}, no group of documents is dense enough for γ=1\gamma = 1, and every document is its own cluster. With CPM, the resolution must be chosen from the distribution of the weights, for instance close to the density of the network for an unweighted graph.

Reading clusters

A cluster is a set of documents with shared references, not an interpretation. Reading it means going back to its documents: what they discuss, when, who wrote them, which references they share, and what distinguishes them from neighbouring clusters (Ding 2011).

Naming clusters with tf-idf

name_clusters() gives each cluster a provisional label. With method = "tf-idf", each cluster is treated as one document made of the titles of its members, and its label gathers the terms with the highest tf-idf (Spärck Jones 1972; Salton and Buckley 1988): terms frequent in the cluster and rare in the others,

tf-idftc=ntc∑unuc×log⁡Cdft, \text{tf-idf}_{tc} = \frac{n_{tc}}{\sum_u n_{uc}} \times \log\frac{C}{\mathrm{df}_t},

with ntcn_{tc} the count of term tt in cluster cc, CC the number of clusters and dft\mathrm{df}_t the number of clusters where tt appears.

network <- name_clusters(
  network,
  method = "tf-idf",
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  text_columns = "source_title",
  nb_terms_label = 3,
  clean_word_method = "lemmatize"
)
node_table <- as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")
clusters <- aggregate(
  as.integer(source_year) ~ cluster_leiden + cluster_label,
  data = node_table,
  FUN = function(year) c(documents = length(year), median_year = median(year))
)
clusters <- do.call(data.frame, clusters)
names(clusters)[3:4] <- c("documents", "median_year")
clusters[order(clusters$median_year), ]
  cluster_leiden                                        cluster_label documents
3             01                     productivity, unemployment, wage        69
4             04                       stagflation, inflation, change         9
2             03                    oil, oil price, great stagflation        18
1             02 great inflation, stabilization, stabilization policy        51
  median_year
3        1980
4        1995
2        2002
1        2005

The labels and the median years already sketch a history. Clusters of the late 1970s and early 1980s talk about productivity, oil, wages and unemployment; clusters centred on the 2000s about the “great inflation” and policy “rules”. This matches the account of Goutsmedt (2021): supply shocks and inflation inertia dominated the first explanations, and a new literature centred on the role of monetary policy emerged in the 1990s. Titles are short, and their words are not always informative (“great”, “comment”): labels are only a first guess. extract_tfidf() shows more terms per cluster, and abstracts, when available, give better labels than titles.

Other methods name a cluster after one of its documents: method = "tidygraph_functions" uses the most central document, for instance by PageRank, and method = "given_column" the document with the highest value of a column, such as the number of citations received.

The role of documents: hubs and bridges

Within a cluster, documents do not play the same role. Guimerà and Nunes Amaral (2005) propose to place each node with two measures. The within-module degree compares the weight κi\kappa_i of the ties of ii with its own cluster sis_i with that of the other members, zi=(κi−κ‾si)/σκsiz_i = (\kappa_i - \bar{\kappa}_{s_i}) / \sigma_{\kappa_{s_i}}. The participation coefficient Pi=1−∑s(kis/ki)2P_i = 1 - \sum_s (k_{is} / k_i)^2, with kisk_{is} the weight of the ties of ii with cluster ss, is 0 when all ties stay in one cluster and approaches 1 when they spread evenly across clusters.

network <- add_node_roles(network, module_col = "cluster_leiden")
roles <- as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")
table(roles$role_ga)

 R1 ultra-peripheral        R2 peripheral R3 non-hub connector
                  12                  125                    9
   R5 provincial hub
                   1 
ggplot(roles, aes(participation_coeff, within_module_z, colour = cluster_label)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 2.5, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scico::scale_colour_scico_d(palette = "batlow") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Participation coefficient", y = "Within-module degree (z-score)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2))

The shaded area holds the hubs of their cluster (z≥2.5z \geq 2.5, the threshold of Guimerà and Amaral). Documents on the right have ties spread over several clusters. The two measures combine into seven roles, which are easier to understand with documents in hand. Here are the documents that best illustrate the roles that exist in this network:

roles |>
  filter(role_ga %in% c("R5 provincial hub", "R6 connector hub", "R3 non-hub connector", "R4 non-hub kinless")) |>
  arrange(role_ga, desc(if_else(grepl("^R[567]", role_ga), within_module_z, participation_coeff))) |>
  group_by(role_ga) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(role = role_ga, document = source_label, title = stringr::str_to_sentence(source_title),
            cluster = cluster_label, z = round(within_module_z, 1), participation = round(participation_coeff, 2)) |>
  as.data.frame()
                  role       document
1 R3 non-hub connector   BALL-L-1995a
2 R3 non-hub connector BLINDER-A-2013
3 R3 non-hub connector  TAYLOR-J-1997
4    R5 provincial hub PINDYCK-R-1980
                                                            title
1               Relative-price changes as aggregate supply shocks
2 The supply-shock explanation of the great stagflation revisited
3            America<92>s peacetime inflation: the 1970s: comment
4                 Energy price increases and macroeconomic policy
                            cluster    z participation
1    stagflation, inflation, change -0.2          0.71
2 oil, oil price, great stagflation  0.1          0.70
3    stagflation, inflation, change -0.2          0.66
4  productivity, unemployment, wage  2.7          0.21

How to read them depends on what the nodes and the ties are. Here, nodes are explanations of the stagflation and ties are shared references:

  • A provincial hub (R5) is the central document of a literature: it shares references with most of the documents of its cluster and with hardly any other. Lansing’s “Exploring the causes of the great inflation”
    1. is one for the cluster on the great inflation, Nordhaus’s “Who’s afraid of a big bad oil shock?” (2007) for the cluster on oil. These are the documents to read first to enter a cluster.
  • A connector hub (R6) is central in its cluster and shares references with others too. Pindyck’s “Energy price increases and macroeconomic policy” (1980) is central in the cluster on productivity, oil and supply while its references also belong to other clusters: a document built on several literatures that remains well embedded in one.
  • A non-hub connector (R3) has ties spread over several clusters without being central in any: a bridge. Blinder’s “The supply-shock explanation of the great stagflation revisited” (2013) belongs to the cluster on oil but shares references with other clusters: it revisits an explanation that earlier documents had built on other bases. In a co-citation network, the same role belongs to works used by several literatures.
  • A non-hub kinless document (R4) spreads its ties evenly over all clusters. This is not a better bridge than R3: it may be an outlier. The only one here, Nitzan’s article on “regimes of differential accumulation” (2001), shares references with each of five clusters in almost equal proportions (17 to 20% of its tie weight in each), and its within-module degree is below the average of its own cluster: it is tied to everybody a little and to nobody much.

Roles are positions in a network, not judgements on the importance of a document. Moreover, they depend on the partition. We recompute the roles for three resolutions of Leiden and follow the five documents above:

resolutions <- c(0.75, 1, 1.5)
by_resolution <- lapply(resolutions, function(resolution) {
  graph <- network |>
    add_clusters(clustering_method = "leiden", objective_function = "modularity",
                 resolution = resolution, seed = 123, verbose = FALSE) |>
    add_node_roles(module_col = "cluster_leiden")
  as_tibble(graph, active = "nodes") |> mutate(resolution = resolution)
})
bind_rows(by_resolution) |>
  group_by(resolution) |>
  summarise(
    clusters = n_distinct(cluster_leiden),
    hubs = sum(role_ga %in% c("R5 provincial hub", "R6 connector hub", "R7 kinless hub")),
    mean_participation = round(mean(participation_coeff), 2)
  ) |>
  as.data.frame()
  resolution clusters hubs mean_participation
1       0.75        3    1               0.25
2       1.00        4    1               0.31
3       1.50        8    2               0.58
bind_rows(by_resolution) |>
  filter(source_label %in% c("LANSING-K-2000a", "NORDHAUS-W-2007", "PINDYCK-R-1980",
                             "BLINDER-A-2013", "NITZAN-J-2001")) |>
  select(document = source_label, resolution, role_ga) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = resolution, values_from = role_ga, names_prefix = "resolution ") |>
  as.data.frame()
         document      resolution 0.75         resolution 1
1  BLINDER-A-2013 R3 non-hub connector R3 non-hub connector
2 LANSING-K-2000a        R2 peripheral        R2 peripheral
3   NITZAN-J-2001 R3 non-hub connector R3 non-hub connector
4 NORDHAUS-W-2007        R2 peripheral        R2 peripheral
5  PINDYCK-R-1980    R5 provincial hub    R5 provincial hub
        resolution 1.5
1   R4 non-hub kinless
2 R3 non-hub connector
3   R4 non-hub kinless
4        R2 peripheral
5     R6 connector hub

With smaller clusters, more ties cross clusters and the participation coefficients increase (the mean goes from 0.31 to 0.52). Blinder stays a connector at the three resolutions, and Lansing a hub, but Pindyck is only a peripheral document (R2) at 0.75 and a connector hub from 1. A role is therefore a statement about a document relative to a given partition: before interpreting a role in a text, check that it survives a reasonable change of resolution. Finally, the thresholds of Guimerà and Amaral were calibrated on metabolic networks. In a network of documents projected from references, a quarter of the pairs are tied, most documents have a participation above 0.05, and hubs are rare (three here): the roles are more useful as a way to find documents to read than as categories to count.

The same measures mean different things for other nodes: in a co-citation network, a hub is a classic cited with most of the works of its literature and a connector a work used by several literatures; for authors coupled through their references (see beyond bibliographic coupling), a connector is an author who cites several literatures.

Drawing the network

Plotting needs coordinates, colours and label positions. layout_networks() computes coordinates with a force-directed layout: here Fruchterman-Reingold (Fruchterman and Reingold 1991), which balances an attraction along edges, stronger for heavier edges, with a repulsion between all nodes. Kamada-Kawai ("kk", Kamada and Kawai (1989)), which draws graph distances as geometric distances, is another common choice, with a trap: igraph reads the weight column as a distance for this layout, so that similarity weights pull weakly tied documents to the margins. With similarity weights, either use "fr" or ignore the weights (weights = NA). color_networks() gives each cluster a colour, and edges a mix of the colours of their ends. plot_networks() assembles the figure.

set.seed(1)
network <- layout_networks(network, node_id = "source_id", layout = "fr")
n_clusters <- length(unique(roles$cluster_leiden))
palette <- data.frame(
  cluster_leiden = sort(unique(roles$cluster_leiden)),
  color = scico::scico(n_clusters, palette = "batlow")
)
network <- color_networks(network, column_to_color = "cluster_leiden", color = palette)
plot_networks(
  network,
  cluster_label_column = "cluster_label",
  node_size_column = NULL
)

Clusters drawn next to each other share more references than clusters at opposite ends, but distances in such a figure should not be measured: the layout is a compromise between many constraints, and another seed gives another, equally valid, picture.

For a closer reading, launch_network_app() opens the same network in an interactive application: clicking a cluster lists its documents with their authors, titles and journals.

launch_network_app(
  graph_tbl = network,
  cluster_id = "cluster_label",
  cluster_information = c("source_author", "source_title", "source_year", "source_journal"),
  node_id = "source_id",
  node_tooltip = "source_label",
  color = "color",
  layout = NULL
)

What comes next

A single network of the whole period mixes literatures that did not coexist. The last guide builds one network per time window and follows the clusters across windows.
